Summary:

In this study, the authors conducted analyses of host and parasite transcription signatures in controlled human malaria infection (CHMI) of naïve subjects with Plasmodium falciparum 3D7 (mainly blood stage parasites). Specifically, the approaches included analyses of immune signatures and transcription of major parasite virulence gene families (var and rif) at various time points before and after very low level infections, which allowed the authors to examine this question in unprecedented detail. The main finding shows that host immune responses vary substantially, influencing time to onset of symptoms, while parasite factors such as replication rates (parasite density) and the absence of marked temporal changes in the expression of variant surface antigens appear not to play a significant role in the initial course of infection. The authors conclude that clinical outcome of CHMI depends on the above-mentioned variation in host immune reactivity rather than transcription of particular var or rif genes.

Although this is well written manuscript describing a study that represents a large body of carefully collected and interpreted data on a topic that is of importance to the malaria community, the conclusion regarding the absence of marked changes in transcripts of var and rif genes is at variance with the current thinking about the pathogenesis of P. falciparum malaria.

Revisions for this paper:

As concerns the current studies, the reviewers are requesting extensive revisions of the manuscript. These revisions are directed at the major aspects of the observations/findings and the authors' data interpretations.

There was a general agreement that the results concerning immune transcripts recapitulated to some extent published data. The data showing Plasmodium gene expression and specifically the absence of any changes in the expression of the var and rif genes generated quite a bit of discussion amongst the reviewers because these results seem at odds what has been reported for host with little malaria experience. In the absence of more definite evidence than what is presented, it is imperative that the authors reduced the rhetoric and entertain a hypothesis that is much better supported by current scientific evidence (i.e., that antigenic variation is very important, indeed). In general, the reviewers agreed that the authors over-interpret their findings on var and rif gene transcription, and not least their significance and therefore, please tone down your claims.

It would have been reassuring, if the authors could demonstrate that the parasites used in the CHMI were indeed capable of changing transcription pattern in response to selection for specific adhesion specificities, in particular adhesion specificities that have been associated with development of severe complications (e.g., adhesion to EPCR or ICAM-1). Without such a capacity, the analysis of parasite gene transcription loses its significance. While the data in Peters et al., 2002, support the authors' assumption that the parasites used can indeed switch, direct evidence would be preferable. Because the experiments that would be most informative are not really feasible, the authors must acknowledge this in the Discussion.

The short duration of the experiment and the relatively small number of participants may simply be insufficient to yield the transcriptomic changes one might expect on the basis of the existing literature. While the authors acknowledge these caveats, they need to consider them in their conclusions, as well as the Abstract. Another point to consider is the parasite density. If the density is the trigger to switch var gene type, then densities may not be high enough in any host. Parasite density is not adequately explored and neither is the contradiction about parasite density and immune status where the inflammatory group had longer infections.

Because the CHMI model necessitated a strict requirement for drug treatment in early infection, it did not essentially recapitulate the natural P. falciparum infection. It is possible, therefore, that in this model there was a critical absence of an important positive feedback loops that would have been activated once inflammation started and which created an environment that may be critical in selection of more virulent parasite types by altering endothelial receptor expression. Again all these are crucial issues to consider, as the present story challenges the existing paradigm of the origins of severe malaria.

1) Please comment on the implications of the shortest infection in immunologically unresponsive participants.

2) Subsection “Systemic inflammation coincides with the onset of clinical symptoms”: Why were only three of eight "inflammatory" volunteers included in the analysis discussed? What was the result when all eight were included?

3) Please include discussion on the role of innate immunity to malaria and the impact of inflammation on the induction of adaptive immunity also should be mentioned.

4) A more expanded information and discussion on parasitological aspects are needed to strengthen the conclusion. Please include the following points in your Discussion/conclusion: parasite multiplication which was the same in the various groups, while Infections lasted longer and parasite densities were higher in the inflammatory group. There appeared to be highly variable density thresholds to induce inflammation, and therefore a possibility exists that there was a hidden or sequestered biomass in some individuals as a consequence of an inflammatory response. Please also comment on the synchronicity of infections in individuals as this will impact the density result.

5) One of the earliest reports, Lavstsen et al., 2005, on var gene transcription in experimental P. falciparum infections, reached a conclusions that transcription of group A and B var genes did increase over early days following CHM. Since these are different conclusions re NF54 parasites from which 3D7 was derived, this point requires a discussion. Bachmann et al., 2019, does not actually study naïve hosts but suggests hosts with existing immunity exert more effect on var gene profiles than non-immune hosts.

6) Subsection “Immune decision-making in falciparum malaria”, second paragraph: are these the same 4 volunteers identified earlier in the same paragraph?

7) Discussion, third paragraph: It is hard to envisage a scenario in which CHMI would be allowed to proceed further due to the inherent risks to the volunteer of rapidly-increasing parasite density.

8) Discussion, fifth paragraph: it seems that inflammation was only present at the time of treatment and one life cycle (48 h) before, based on Figure 1 – so it may be that there was not enough time for inflammation-mediated alterations in host receptor expression to feed through into the var gene profiles by providing a selective advantage to certain adhesive types.

9) "as part of a custom-design multiplex assay from BioLegend" – does that mean other markers were also measured and were not informative? This would be useful to know given the emphasis on an "inflammatory" response when there is no evidence of classic inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL1 etc.).

10) Subsection “Analysis of parasite var and rifin expression”: were the var reads measured on each of these three days (9, 10, 11)? The Materials and methods don't seem to state which day the samples from the blood challenge were collected for var analysis, although it seems clear from results.

11) Please comment on the relevance of these finding to clinical vaccine and drug trials.

12) Please revise the title of your manuscript to reflect the changes in your revised manuscript

Revisions expected in follow-up work:

Given how challenging this work has been, no additional experiments are being suggested for this study, but repeating similar studies with different parasite lines and eventually in malaria endemic areas would be important to consider for future experiments.

claims.claim: There was no transcriptional evidence for preferential expansion of group A or DC8 var genes in naive hosts.
claims.source: When we tracked temporal changes in parasite VSA expression to ask whether variants associated with severe disease rapidly expand in naive hosts, we found no transcriptional evidence to support this hypothesis.

claims.claim: Parasite variants that dominate severe malaria do not have an intrinsic growth or survival advantage.
claims.source: These data indicate that parasite variants that dominate severe malaria do not have an intrinsic growth or survival advantage; instead, they presumably rely upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment for selection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of preferential expansion of group A/DC8 variants during the study period.

claims.claim: Parasite variants associated with severe disease rely upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment for selection.

claims.claim: There is enormous diversity in the human response to identical immune challenge.
claims.source: There is enormous diversity in the human response to identical immune challenge.
claims.evidence: This is supported by references to large cohort studies examining immune variation.

claims.claim: Heterogeneity in the host response to Plasmodium falciparum is well-recognised.
claims.source: Controlled human malaria infection (CHMI) provides a well-established challenge model in which to examine immune variation in vivo, and heterogeneity in the host response to Plasmodium falciparum is well-recognised (Roestenberg et al., 2012; Yap et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CHMI studies.

claims.claim: Prior work suggests a dichotomy in immune decision-making with some individuals triggering an inflammatory response characterized by high circulating levels of IFNγ.
claims.source: Prior work suggests a dichotomy in immune decision-making with some individuals triggering an inflammatory response, which is characterised by high circulating levels of IFNγ, whilst others mount an alternative response distinguished by the early release of TGFβ and suppression of IFNγ signalling (de Jong et al., 2020; Harpaz et al., 1992; Walther et al., 2005; Walther et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Some individuals mount an alternative response distinguished by the early release of TGFβ and suppression of IFNγ signalling.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The precise mechanisms underpinning divergent immune responses remain unknown.

claims.claim: Previous CHMI studies have revealed an upregulation of genes associated with pathogen detection, NFκB activation, and IFNγ signalling consistent with a systemic inflammatory response.
claims.source: Genome-wide transcriptional profiling has the potential to map immune decision-making in unprecedented detail and previous CHMI studies have revealed an upregulation of genes associated with pathogen detection, NFκB activation, and IFNγ signalling consistent with a systemic inflammatory response (Ockenhouse et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous transcriptional profiling studies.

claims.claim: A transcriptional signature of an alternative immune response has not been described in naive hosts.

claims.claim: Direct intravenous challenge with blood-stage parasites ensures all volunteers receive an identical immune challenge.
claims.source: In this context, direct intravenous challenge with blood-stage parasites provides a unique opportunity to assess the contribution of host-intrinsic mechanisms of variation as it ensures all volunteers receive an identical immune challenge (Duncan and Draper, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and is a characteristic of the blood challenge model.

claims.claim: Expression of group A and DC8 var genes is associated with severe malaria in both children and adults.
claims.source: Expression of a subset of parasite variant surface antigens (VSA) known as group A and DC8 var genes is associated with severe malaria in both children and adults (Duffy et al., 2019; Jespersen et al., 2016; Kyriacou et al., 2006; Lavstsen et al., 2012; Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018; Warimwe et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claims.claim: Group A and DC8 var genes encode PfEMP1 adhesion molecules that mediate sequestration of infected red cells in the microvasculature.
claims.source: These virulence-associated genes encode PfEMP1 adhesion molecules that mediate sequestration of infected red cells in the microvasculature.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claims.claim: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites are thought to be more pathogenic than those expressing other var types (groups B and C).
claims.source: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites are thought to be more pathogenic than those expressing other var types (groups B and C) and can bind the endothelium with high affinity in sensitive sites, such as brain (Jensen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and represents current understanding in the field.

claims.claim: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites can bind the endothelium with high affinity in sensitive sites, such as brain.
claims.source: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites are thought to be more pathogenic than those expressing other var types (groups B and C) and can bind the endothelium with high affinity in sensitive sites, such as brain (Jensen et al., 2020).

claims.claim: It is unknown whether expression of group A/DC8 variants can influence the immune response.
claims.source: It is unknown whether expression of these variants can influence the immune response, for example by causing dysregulated activation that leads to widespread collateral tissue damage.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claims.claim: It is unknown whether inflammation might preferentially support the survival and expansion of group A/DC8 variants by upregulating their binding sites on the endothelium.
claims.source: Or conversely, whether inflammation might preferentially support the survival and expansion of these variants by upregulating their binding sites on the endothelium.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about an unanswered question in the field.

claims.claim: Parasites transcribe a broad array of var genes in naive hosts, with predominant expression of group B variants and no marked differences between volunteers.
claims.source: It has been observed in previous CHMI studies that parasites transcribe a broad array of var genes in naive hosts, with predominant expression of group B variants and no marked differences between volunteers (Bachmann et al., 2019; Bachmann et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CHMI studies.

claims.claim: Mosquitoes reset malaria parasites to ensure diverse expression of their VSA repertoire at the start of the blood cycle.
claims.source: Indeed, we have shown that mosquitoes reset malaria parasites to ensure diverse expression of their VSA repertoire at the start of the blood cycle (Spence et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: It remains unclear how group A and DC8 var genes come to dominate the PfEMP1 landscape in severe malaria.
claims.source: It therefore remains unclear how group A and DC8 var genes come to dominate the PfEMP1 landscape in severe malaria.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about an unresolved question in the field.

claims.claim: Antibody-mediated clearance of parasites expressing group B variants is unlikely to explain dominance of group A/DC8 variants because severe malaria develops in hosts with low or absent immunity during their first few infections of life.
claims.source: Antibody-mediated clearance of parasites expressing group B variants is a possible explanation, but is unlikely because severe malaria develops in hosts with low or absent immunity during their first few infections of life (Gonçalves et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claims.claim: It has been suggested that parasites expressing group A/DC8 var genes rapidly and preferentially expand because they have an intrinsic growth and/or survival advantage in naive hosts.
claims.source: It has instead been suggested that parasites expressing group A/DC8 var genes rapidly and preferentially expand because they have an intrinsic growth and/or survival advantage in naive hosts (Abdi et al., 2017; Bull et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous hypotheses in the literature.

claims.claim: The hypothesis that group A/DC8 variants have an intrinsic growth advantage is widely accepted but is not based on substantial evidence.
claims.source: This explanation is widely accepted but is not based on substantial evidence.
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of the current state of evidence.

claims.claim: A cohort of 14 malaria-naive volunteers were infected with an equal number of blood-stage parasites (clone 3D7) by direct intravenous inoculation.
claims.source: To explore host-intrinsic variation in the immune response to P. falciparum, a cohort of 14 malaria-naive volunteers were infected with an equal number of blood-stage parasites (clone 3D7) by direct intravenous inoculation (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claims.claim: The pathogenic blood cycle was initiated in every volunteer within a 30-min window.
claims.source: This enabled the pathogenic blood cycle to be initiated in every volunteer within a 30-min window (Payne et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and describes a feature of the blood challenge model.

claims.claim: Systemic changes in the host response were captured through time by transcriptionally profiling whole blood every 48 hr from the day before infection until the day of diagnosis.
claims.source: Systemic changes in the host response were then captured through time by transcriptionally profiling whole blood every 48 hr from the day before infection until the day of diagnosis (the point of drug treatment).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: The time-point of diagnosis varied between volunteers, occurring 7.5–10.5 days post-infection.
claims.source: This time-point varied between volunteers, occurring 7.5–10.5 days post-infection when two out of three diagnostic criteria were met (positive thick blood smear and/or parasite density >500 parasites ml−1 by qPCR and/or symptoms consistent with malaria).
claims.evidence: This describes the variability in time to diagnosis in the study.

claims.claim: Variance in one third of infected volunteers (4/14) was comparable to the uninfected control group.
claims.source: We found that variance in one third of infected volunteers (4/14) was comparable to the uninfected control group, suggesting these four volunteers did not respond to infection (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression variance.

claims.claim: Four volunteers (v018, v012, v208, and v020) failed to cross both thresholds for a measurable response and were therefore grouped and labelled unresponsive.
claims.source: Using the variance and distance travelled metrics, we then set two thresholds to identify volunteers that triggered a measurable response to blood challenge (see Materials and methods); four volunteers failed to cross both thresholds (v018, v012, v208, and v020) and were therefore grouped and labelled unresponsive.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of transcriptional data.

claims.claim: There were zero differentially expressed genes in the unresponsive group at diagnosis compared to pre-infection.
claims.source: A pairwise comparison between the diagnosis and pre-infection samples obtained from these four volunteers confirmed that there were zero differentially expressed genes in this group (adj p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Immune quiescence is a common outcome of controlled human malaria infection.
claims.source: Immune quiescence is therefore a common outcome of controlled human malaria infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the finding that 4/14 volunteers showed no response.

claims.claim: The remaining 10 volunteers made a robust response to infection based on variance and distance travelled metrics.
claims.source: In contrast, variance (Figure 1—source data 1) and distance travelled (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) both suggested that the remaining 10 volunteers made a robust response to infection (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transcriptional data.

claims.claim: Eight volunteers upregulated gene clusters 2 and 4 at diagnosis.
claims.source: Based on this observation, we grouped the eight volunteers who upregulated gene clusters 2 and 4 and performed a pairwise comparison between their diagnosis and pre-infection samples; we uncovered 2028 differentially expressed genes (adj p<0.05) (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis and differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: 2028 genes were differentially expressed at diagnosis in the inflammatory group compared to pre-infection.
claims.source: Based on this observation, we grouped the eight volunteers who upregulated gene clusters 2 and 4 and performed a pairwise comparison between their diagnosis and pre-infection samples; we uncovered 2028 differentially expressed genes (adj p<0.05) (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: ClueGO uncovered 217 GO terms across 34 functional groups for the inflammatory response.
claims.source: ClueGO uncovered 217 GO terms across 34 functional groups (Supplementary file 4); the most significant groups related to interferon signalling, activation of myeloid cells, production of inflammatory molecules, and activation of T cells (Figure 2a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis using ClueGO.

claims.claim: The most significant functional groups in the inflammatory response related to interferon signalling, activation of myeloid cells, production of inflammatory molecules, and activation of T cells.
claims.source: ClueGO uncovered 217 GO terms across 34 functional groups (Supplementary file 4); the most significant groups related to interferon signalling, activation of myeloid cells, production of inflammatory molecules, and activation of T cells (Figure 2a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis.

claims.claim: There was a > 2-fold increase in CXCL9 and/or CXCL10 at diagnosis in every volunteer in the inflammatory group but no other volunteer.
claims.source: We then biologically validated ClueGO's in silico finding by measuring the plasma concentrations of two interferon-stimulated chemokines, CXCL9 and CXCL10. These chemokines are primarily produced by myeloid cells and specifically function to recruit and activate T cells (Groom and Luster, 2011). We found a > 2-fold increase in one or both of these chemokines at diagnosis in every volunteer in this group but no other volunteer (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by plasma protein measurements.

claims.claim: CXCL9 and CXCL10 are primarily produced by myeloid cells and specifically function to recruit and activate T cells.
claims.source: These chemokines are primarily produced by myeloid cells and specifically function to recruit and activate T cells (Groom and Luster, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about these chemokines.

claims.claim: Two volunteers were grouped as suppressors based on their apparent downregulation of clusters 1 and 3 at diagnosis.
claims.source: The final two volunteers were also grouped (and given the suppressor tag) based on their apparent downregulation of clusters 1 and 3 at diagnosis (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of gene expression data.

claims.claim: 77 genes were differentially expressed in the suppressor group at diagnosis compared to pre-infection.
claims.source: Significantly, a pairwise comparison between their diagnosis and pre-infection samples revealed a core signature of 77 genes that were differentially expressed in response to blood challenge (adj p<0.05, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: The majority of differentially expressed genes in the suppressor group (62/77) were downregulated.
claims.source: The majority of these genes (62/77) were downregulated and crucially >85% were unique to this group, including key regulators of monocyte and neutrophil differentiation (Csf3r) and recruitment and activation (Cxcl7, Cxcr2, Clec4e, Clec7a, and Mnda, Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: >85% of differentially expressed genes in the suppressor group were unique to this group.
claims.source: The majority of these genes (62/77) were downregulated and crucially >85% were unique to this group, including key regulators of monocyte and neutrophil differentiation (Csf3r) and recruitment and activation (Cxcl7, Cxcr2, Clec4e, Clec7a, and Mnda, Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of differentially expressed genes between groups.

claims.claim: 893 genes were differentially expressed between the inflammatory and suppressor groups at diagnosis.
claims.source: A direct pairwise comparison between the inflammatory and suppressor groups confirmed that each of these six immune genes was differentially expressed at diagnosis, together with a further 887 genes (adj p<0.05, Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis (6 + 887 = 893).

claims.claim: The host response profiles of inflammatory and suppressor groups do not overlap and likely represent distinct in vivo outcomes of immune decision-making.
claims.source: Evidently, these host response profiles do not overlap and instead likely represent distinct in vivo outcomes of immune decision-making.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential gene expression analysis showing distinct signatures.

claims.claim: There are at least three possible outcomes of blood-stage infection: immune quiescence, interferon-stimulated inflammation, and suppression of myeloid-associated gene expression.
claims.source: Collectively, these data reveal marked variation in the human immune response to falciparum malaria with at least three possible outcomes of blood-stage infection – immune quiescence, interferon-stimulated inflammation, and suppression of myeloid-associated gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the transcriptional profiling data.

claims.claim: Five additional malaria-naive volunteers were inoculated with the same parasite genotype by mosquito bite.
claims.source: We therefore inoculated five additional malaria-naive volunteers with the same parasite genotype but this time by the natural route of infection, mosquito bite (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the mosquito challenge study.

claims.claim: 116 out of 117 genes in the 117-gene superset were upregulated exclusively during the blood cycle after mosquito challenge.
claims.source: When we clustered and visualised the expression data within this superset we found that 116 out of 117 genes were upregulated exclusively during the blood cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data from mosquito challenge.

claims.claim: Response to interferon gamma (GO: 0034341) was the most significantly enriched GO term in the 117-gene superset from mosquito challenge.
claims.source: And when we examined the biological functions of these genes ClueGO identified response to interferon gamma (GO: 0034341) as the most significantly enriched GO term (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis.

claims.claim: Response to interferon gamma was also the most significant GO term in inflammatory volunteers infected by blood challenge.
claims.source: Notably, this was also the most significant GO term in inflammatory volunteers infected by blood challenge (Supplementary file 4), indicating concordance between the two infection models.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of gene ontology analyses between the two studies.

claims.claim: 19 of the 21 genes that displayed the highest fold change in inflammatory volunteers (blood challenge) were also upregulated in the 117-gene superset (mosquito challenge).
claims.source: In agreement, 19 of the 21 genes that displayed the highest fold change in inflammatory volunteers (blood challenge) were also upregulated in the 117-gene superset (mosquito challenge, Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of gene expression data between the two studies.

claims.claim: High circulating levels of CXCL10 were detectable at diagnosis in four of the five volunteers infected by mosquito bite.
claims.source: And at protein level, high circulating levels of CXCL10 were detectable at diagnosis in four of the five volunteers infected by mosquito bite (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by plasma protein measurements.

claims.claim: Interferon-stimulated inflammation is the dominant human response to blood-stage parasites regardless of the route of infection.
claims.source: Our data therefore demonstrate that interferon-stimulated inflammation is the dominant human response to blood-stage parasites regardless of the route of infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the concordance between blood and mosquito challenge studies.

claims.claim: The data fail to provide compelling evidence of a systemic transcriptional response to liver-stage infection in human malaria.
claims.source: Furthermore, our data fail to provide compelling evidence of a systemic transcriptional response to liver-stage infection in human malaria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This is based on the observation that gene expression changes occurred only during the blood cycle.

claims.claim: The pre-erythrocytic-stages of infection may have a limited role in shaping the immune response during the pathogenic blood cycle.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the pre-erythrocytic-stages of infection may have a limited role in shaping the immune response during the pathogenic blood cycle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional response during liver-stage infection.

claims.claim: The parasite multiplication rate varied considerably between volunteers (range 6.7–12.8).
claims.source: The parasite multiplication rate (PMR, modelled from the qPCR data [Payne et al., 2016]) varied considerably between volunteers (range 6.7–12.8) despite every individual receiving an equal number of infected red cells (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and modeling.

claims.claim: The parasite multiplication rate of the inflammatory group was not significantly different to that of unresponsive or suppressor hosts.
claims.source: However, the parasite multiplication rate of the inflammatory group was not significantly different to that of unresponsive or suppressor hosts (Figure 3a–b) and therefore appears to have little bearing on the outcome of immune decision-making.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of parasite multiplication rates between groups.

claims.claim: Inflammatory volunteers tended to have a longer course of infection.
claims.source: Inflammatory volunteers did, however, tend to have a longer course of infection (Figure 3a) and hence the parasite burden at diagnosis was higher for the inflammatory group (median 30,309 parasites ml−1, range 9133–273,247) than the rest of the cohort (median 7899 parasites ml−1, range 1440–19,670) (Mann Whitney test, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of time to diagnosis and parasite density data.

claims.claim: The parasite burden at diagnosis was higher for the inflammatory group (median 30,309 parasites ml−1) than the rest of the cohort (median 7899 parasites ml−1).
claims.source: Inflammatory volunteers did, however, tend to have a longer course of infection (Figure 3a) and hence the parasite burden at diagnosis was higher for the inflammatory group (median 30,309 parasites ml−1, range 9133–273,247) than the rest of the cohort (median 7899 parasites ml−1, range 1440–19,670) (Mann Whitney test, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of parasite densities.

claims.claim: Parasite burden may promote an inflammatory response in the blood challenge model but cannot fully explain it.
claims.source: Parasite burden may therefore promote an inflammatory response in this challenge model but cannot fully explain it; for example, 2/4 unresponsive volunteers (v018 and v020) had parasite densities that were comparable to 4/8 inflammatory volunteers at diagnosis (v017, v027, v026, and v106, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some unresponsive volunteers had similar parasite densities to inflammatory volunteers.

claims.claim: The parasite density threshold required to trigger inflammation is highly variable between individuals.
claims.source: Our data therefore support previous observations that the parasite density threshold required to trigger inflammation is highly variable between individuals (Gatton and Cheng, 2002; Molineaux et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the current data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Volunteers in the unresponsive and suppressor groups were essentially asymptomatic at diagnosis.
claims.source: Volunteers in the unresponsive and suppressor groups were essentially asymptomatic at diagnosis, whereas inflammatory volunteers exhibited more frequent and/or severe adverse events, including fever (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clinical symptom data.

claims.claim: Inflammatory volunteers exhibited more frequent and/or severe adverse events, including fever.
claims.source: Volunteers in the unresponsive and suppressor groups were essentially asymptomatic at diagnosis, whereas inflammatory volunteers exhibited more frequent and/or severe adverse events, including fever (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clinical symptom data.

claims.claim: There was a strong positive correlation between symptoms and the intensity of inflammation.
claims.source: When we then calculated a cumulative clinical score for each volunteer (by summing all adverse events throughout infection) we found a strong positive correlation between symptoms and the intensity of inflammation (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between clinical score and parasite multiplication rate.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no correlation between clinical score and parasite multiplication rate (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Only one volunteer displayed elevated levels of Angiopoietin-2, and this individual was the most inflammatory host in the cohort.
claims.source: We then measured circulating levels of Angiopoietin-2, a biomarker of endothelium dysfunction and indicator of disease severity (Yeo et al., 2008); only one volunteer displayed elevated levels of Angiopoietin-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and this individual was the most inflammatory host in the cohort (based on upregulation of plasma CXCL10 and IFNγ).
claims.evidence: This is supported by plasma protein measurements.

claims.claim: Only inflammatory volunteers experienced acute lymphopenia, a conserved hallmark of clinical malaria.
claims.source: What's more, haematological analysis revealed that only inflammatory volunteers experienced acute lymphopenia, a conserved hallmark of clinical malaria (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–d; Hviid et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by haematological data and citation.

claims.claim: Symptomatology is not driven by the rate of parasite replication in controlled human malaria infection.
claims.source: Symptomatology is therefore not driven by the rate of parasite replication in controlled human malaria infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between clinical score and parasite multiplication rate.

claims.claim: Clinical outcome depends upon the intensity of inflammation, which varies widely between hosts.
claims.source: Instead, clinical outcome seems to depend upon the intensity of inflammation, which varies widely between hosts.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation between inflammation and symptoms.

claims.claim: No metabolic signature of inflammation was robust to multiple testing when comparing inflammatory to unresponsive and suppressor hosts.
claims.source: When we compared the three most inflammatory and symptomatic volunteers to unresponsive and suppressor hosts we could find no metabolic signature of inflammation that was robust to multiple testing (zero metabolites with an FDR-corrected p value < 0.1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS metabolomics analysis.

claims.claim: A conserved and persistent signature of blood-stage infection was characterized by increased adenosine, choline depletion and reduced lysoPC.
claims.source: On the other hand, if we simply considered all volunteers as a single group and compared their post-infection time-points (day 8 and diagnosis) against pre-infection samples we could identify a conserved and persistent signature of blood-stage infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). This was characterised by increased adenosine (promotes vasodilation [Ralevic and Dunn, 2015]), choline depletion (supports parasite membrane synthesis [Witola and Ben Mamoun, 2007]) and reduced lysoPC (induces gametocytogenesis [Brancucci et al., 2017, Figure 3e–f]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS metabolomics analysis.

claims.claim: Volunteers who are immune quiescent are metabolically responsive to P. falciparum, and their response is indistinguishable from inflammatory hosts.
claims.source: Evidently, volunteers who are immune quiescent are nevertheless metabolically responsive to P. falciparum, and their response is indistinguishable from inflammatory hosts.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the shared metabolic signature across all volunteers.

claims.claim: Immune decision-making, systemic metabolism and parasite replication all operate independently in the early stages of the blood cycle.
claims.source: All together, these data reveal that immune decision-making, systemic metabolism and parasite replication all operate independently in the early stages of the blood cycle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between these different parameters.

claims.claim: There is a clear relationship between the intensity of inflammation and symptomatology in falciparum malaria.
claims.source: And they further reveal a clear relationship between the intensity of inflammation and symptomatology in falciparum malaria.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis between inflammation markers and clinical scores.

claims.claim: The inoculum used for blood challenge derived from a single malaria-infected volunteer infected by mosquito bite and was cryopreserved ex vivo after just three cycles of asexual replication.
claims.source: In the first instance, we examined the hierarchy of var gene expression in the inoculum used for blood challenge; this derived from a single malaria-infected volunteer infected by mosquito bite and was cryopreserved ex vivo (without culture) after just three cycles of asexual replication (Cheng et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This describes the source and preparation of the inoculum.

claims.claim: More than 20 var genes were highly transcribed in the inoculum.
claims.source: In agreement, we found more than 20 var genes highly transcribed in the inoculum; notably, the expression hierarchy was dominated by group B variants and there was very low (or undetectable) transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the inoculum.

claims.claim: The expression hierarchy in the inoculum was dominated by group B variants.
claims.source: In agreement, we found more than 20 var genes highly transcribed in the inoculum; notably, the expression hierarchy was dominated by group B variants and there was very low (or undetectable) transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the inoculum.

claims.claim: There was very low or undetectable transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes in the inoculum.
claims.source: In agreement, we found more than 20 var genes highly transcribed in the inoculum; notably, the expression hierarchy was dominated by group B variants and there was very low (or undetectable) transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the inoculum.

claims.claim: PF3D7_0400400 encodes a group A brain endothelial cell binding PfEMP1 variant.
claims.source: One exception was PF3D7_0400400 (previously PFD0020c), which encodes a group A brain endothelial cell binding PfEMP1 variant (Claessens et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study characterizing this variant.

claims.claim: Group B var genes dominated the PfEMP1 landscape when parasites were isolated from the mosquito challenge cohort.
claims.source: We further found that group B var genes dominated the PfEMP1 landscape when parasites were isolated from our mosquito challenge cohort, albeit with a higher proportion of var gene reads mapping to group A and with two DC8-like variants highly transcribed in some volunteers (PF3D7_0600200 (aka PFF0010w) and PF3D7_0800300 (aka PF08_0140)) (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b and Figure 4—source data 1).

results.result: The study identified three distinct host immune response patterns to blood-stage P. falciparum infection: immune quiescence (4/14 volunteers with zero differentially expressed genes), interferon-stimulated inflammation (8/14 volunteers with 2028 differentially expressed genes enriched for interferon signaling and myeloid activation), and myeloid suppression (2/14 volunteers with 77 differentially expressed genes, 62 downregulated, including key myeloid regulators).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C38-C55 collectively demonstrate three distinct immune response patterns using multiple complementary approaches: variance analysis (C38-C40), differential gene expression (C43-C44, C50-C51), gene ontology enrichment (C45-C46), and protein validation (C47). The classification criteria are clearly defined with quantitative thresholds, and the biological validation of inflammatory markers (CXCL9/CXCL10) strengthens the transcriptional findings. The statistical analysis (adj p<0.05) and the distinct gene expression profiles between groups (C53-C54) provide robust support for three separate immune outcomes.

results.result: Only inflammatory volunteers experienced hallmark symptoms of malaria, with a strong positive correlation between inflammation intensity (measured by CXCL10) and cumulative clinical score (p=5×10⁻⁴), but no correlation between symptoms and parasite multiplication rate (p=0.976). Inflammatory volunteers also exhibited fever, acute lymphopenia, and one volunteer showed elevated Angiopoietin-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C71-C78, C83 are well-supported by clinical data, correlation analyses, and hematological measurements. The strong statistical correlation between CXCL10 and clinical score (C73) contrasts with the absence of correlation with parasite multiplication rate (C74), providing clear evidence that symptomatology depends on inflammation intensity rather than parasite replication rate. The clinical observations (fever, lymphopenia) and biomarker data (Angiopoietin-2) provide convergent evidence. However, the sample size is small (n=14) and one outlier (v016) drives some of the biomarker findings (C75).

results.result: After six cycles of replication in blood challenge, there was no preferential expansion of group A or DC8 var genes. The expression hierarchy remained dominated by group B variants (particularly PF3D7_1041300), with group A/DC8 variants remaining low or undetectable at diagnosis. Differential gene expression analysis confirmed no var gene was more highly transcribed at the end versus start of infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C85-C87, C92-C97 provide strong evidence against preferential expansion of virulence-associated variants using RNA-sequencing at the start (inoculum) and end (diagnosis) of infection. The analysis of intron-spanning reads (C95) specifically demonstrates loss of functional transcription of the group A variant PF3D7_0400400. The DESeq2 analysis (C96, adj p<0.01) provides statistical rigor. However, the study is limited to one parasite genotype (3D7) and a short infection window (~6 cycles), which the authors acknowledge. The ex vivo methodology avoids culture artifacts but may miss rare switching events.

results.result: The authors conclude that parasite variants dominating severe malaria do not have an intrinsic growth or survival advantage; instead, their preferential expansion relies upon infection-induced changes in the within-host environment, with responsibility for severe malaria shared between parasite and host.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C130-C131 represent speculative conclusions based on the absence of var gene switching/selection observed in the study (C7, C97). While the negative result is well-documented, the inference that group A/DC8 variants have NO intrinsic advantage is not definitively proven—the study may simply have been too short (6 cycles) or used a parasite line with altered switching behavior. The proposed alternative mechanism (environmental selection) is plausible but not directly tested. The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations in the discussion, but the claims remain inferential rather than demonstrated.

results.result: Comparison of mosquito bite versus blood challenge showed that 116/117 genes in the inflammatory signature were upregulated exclusively during the blood cycle (not liver stage), with interferon gamma response as the most enriched GO term in both infection routes. High CXCL10 levels were detected in 4/5 mosquito-challenged volunteers, indicating interferon-stimulated inflammation is the dominant response regardless of infection route, and pre-erythrocytic stages have limited role in shaping the blood-stage immune response.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C64 are supported by concordant transcriptional and protein data from two independent infection routes. The gene expression analysis (C57-C60) shows strong overlap between blood and mosquito challenge, and the protein validation (C61) confirms the transcriptional findings. However, the conclusion about limited liver-stage contribution (C63-C64) is based on absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence—the study may lack power to detect subtle liver-stage responses. The sample size for mosquito challenge is small (n=5) and only one uninfected control was available.

results.result: Parasite multiplication rate varied considerably (range 6.7-12.8) but was not significantly different between inflammatory and other volunteers (p=0.681). However, inflammatory volunteers had longer infections and higher parasite burden at diagnosis (median 30,309 vs 7,899 parasites/ml, p=0.02). Parasite burden may promote inflammation but cannot fully explain it, as some unresponsive volunteers had densities comparable to inflammatory volunteers.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by qPCR data, statistical modeling, and appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney). The key finding that parasite multiplication rate does not predict immune response (C66) is well-demonstrated, though the higher parasite burden in inflammatory volunteers (C68) introduces a potential confounding factor. The observation that some unresponsive volunteers had high parasite densities (C69) strengthens the conclusion that parasite density alone cannot explain immune outcomes. However, the causal relationship between longer infection duration and higher parasite burden versus inflammation remains unclear.

results.result: No metabolic signature of inflammation was robust to multiple testing when comparing inflammatory to unresponsive/suppressor hosts. However, all volunteers shared a conserved metabolic response characterized by increased adenosine, choline depletion, and reduced lysoPC. Immune quiescent volunteers were metabolically responsive to P. falciparum, with responses indistinguishable from inflammatory hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by LC-MS metabolomics data with appropriate statistical corrections (FDR<0.1). The absence of an inflammation-specific metabolic signature (C79) is a negative result but is clearly stated with the statistical threshold. The shared metabolic response (C80) is well-documented with authentic standards validating key metabolites. However, the sample size is small (n=7 volunteers analyzed) and the biological interpretation of the metabolic changes relies on cited literature rather than direct functional validation in this study.

results.result: There were no differentially expressed var or rifin genes between inflammatory volunteers and the rest of the cohort. Only one parasite gene (Pfck1, encoding casein kinase one) was differentially expressed (log2 FC=7.32, adj p=0.002), being more highly transcribed in inflammatory volunteers. The diverse clinical outcomes cannot be easily explained by parasite gene expression variation and must largely originate from host-intrinsic immune variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by DESeq2 analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (adj p<0.01). The finding of only one differentially expressed parasite gene (Pfck1) is striking and well-documented. However, the conclusion that clinical outcomes 'must largely originate from host-intrinsic immune variation' (C103) is somewhat overstated—the analysis is limited to transcriptional data and may miss post-transcriptional regulation, protein-level differences, or parasite phenotypes not captured by RNA-seq. The Pfck1 finding (C100-C101) is intriguing but requires validation in independent studies.

results.result: The study design involved 14 malaria-naive volunteers infected with equal numbers of blood-stage parasites (clone 3D7) by direct intravenous inoculation, initiating the blood cycle within a 30-minute window. Whole blood was transcriptionally profiled every 48 hours from day -1 until diagnosis (7.5-10.5 days post-infection), ensuring all volunteers received an identical immune challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37, C21 accurately describe the experimental design, which is well-documented in the methods and supplementary materials. The blood challenge model is appropriately cited (C35, C21) and the standardization of the inoculum and timing is a key strength. The variable time to diagnosis (C37) is clearly defined by objective criteria. This represents sound experimental design for studying host-intrinsic variation.

results.result: The inoculum was derived from a single volunteer infected by mosquito bite and cryopreserved after three cycles of replication. More than 20 var genes were highly transcribed, dominated by group B variants with very low group A/DC8 transcription (except PF3D7_0400400, a group A brain-binding variant). In mosquito challenge, group B variants also dominated, though with higher group A proportions and two DC8-like variants (PF3D7_0600200, PF3D7_0800300) highly transcribed in some volunteers.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 are supported by RNA-sequencing data from both inoculum and mosquito challenge samples. The characterization of var gene expression hierarchies is thorough and includes appropriate citations for variant classifications (C88). The observation that parasites exit the liver with diverse var expression dominated by group B variants (C91) confirms previous findings. The methodology (ex vivo, no culture) is a strength, though the reliance on a single parasite genotype (3D7) limits generalizability.

results.result: The authors propose that environmental changes (inflammation, tissue damage, metabolic disturbance, endothelium activation) lead to rapid selection of severe disease-associated variants rather than increased switching rates. In theory, inflammation could select for group A/DC8 variants through cytokine-mediated upregulation of endothelial receptors like ICAM-1 (upregulated by TNF), enhancing cytoadherence and reducing splenic clearance compared to group B/C variants that bind only CD36. However, plasma TNF had not yet increased at diagnosis in this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C129, C132-C136 represent a proposed mechanistic hypothesis that is plausible and supported by cited literature (C133, C135) but not directly tested in this study. The observation that TNF had not increased at diagnosis (C136) actually argues against the proposed mechanism operating within the study timeframe. The hypothesis is speculative (C129, C132 are labeled as 'theory' and 'prediction') and would require additional experiments (e.g., extended infection duration, endothelial receptor expression analysis) to validate. The authors appropriately present this as a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Parasites from inflammatory volunteers expressed higher levels of Pfck1, a serine-threonine kinase shown to regulate pathogen virulence in leishmaniasis and toxoplasmosis, which may be able to directly regulate type I interferon signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are based on a single differentially expressed gene (C100) with the functional interpretation relying entirely on studies in other pathogens (leishmaniasis, toxoplasmosis). While the differential expression is statistically significant (log2 FC=7.32, adj p=0.002), no functional validation of Pfck1's role in malaria or its effect on interferon signaling was performed in this study. The authors appropriately describe this as 'intriguing' and note it requires validation in a separate study. The claim about interferon regulation (C141) is particularly speculative ('may be able to').

results.result: The manuscript establishes the context that falciparum malaria is clinically heterogeneous, the relative contribution of parasite and host to disease severity remains unclear, and several key mechanistic questions are unresolved, including how group A/DC8 var genes come to dominate severe malaria and whether these variants influence or are influenced by the immune response.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C11, C14, C16, C26-C27, C30, C33 accurately represent the current state of knowledge in the field and are appropriately supported by citations or represent acknowledged gaps. These claims establish the rationale for the study and are consistent with the malaria literature. The critical assessment that the intrinsic growth advantage hypothesis is 'widely accepted but not based on substantial evidence' (C33) is a fair characterization that motivates the experimental work.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about var genes: group A/DC8 variants are associated with severe malaria, encode PfEMP1 molecules mediating sequestration, are thought to be more pathogenic, and can bind brain endothelium with high affinity. Previous CHMI studies showed parasites transcribe diverse var genes in naive hosts with predominant group B expression, and mosquitoes reset parasites to ensure diverse VSA expression. The hypothesis that group A/DC8 variants have intrinsic growth advantages has been suggested but antibody-mediated clearance is unlikely to explain their dominance.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25, C28-C29, C31-C32 accurately summarize prior work with appropriate citations. These are well-established findings in the malaria field (C22-C25) or represent previous observations from CHMI studies (C28-C29). The critical evaluation of competing hypotheses (C31-C32) is fair and appropriately cited. These claims provide essential background but do not represent new findings from this study.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings with epidemiological observations that severe malaria manifestations depend on host age, children learn to tolerate high parasite densities, blood-stage parasites trigger interferon signaling in bone marrow, and the observed transcriptional changes likely reflect activated myeloid cells trafficking to spleen. The discussion also notes that immunity to severe malaria can be acquired early in life and most immune variation is underpinned by non-heritable factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110, C113, C121-C122, C142-C143 represent appropriate contextualization of the study findings with cited epidemiological and immunological literature. The interpretation that transcriptional changes reflect myeloid cell trafficking (C107) is a reasonable inference based on cited work (C106) and the observed gene expression patterns. The discussion of pyrogenic thresholds (C113) and non-heritable immune variation (C143) appropriately frames the study's findings in the broader literature. These are interpretive claims that are well-supported by citations.

results.result: The discussion addresses study limitations and alternative explanations: a previous study suggesting early var switching may have been confounded by in vitro culture; the current study's ex vivo approach avoids this bias but has limitations; the 3D7 line has retained switching capacity based on prior work and variation in group A/DC8 expression in mosquito challenge; CHMI volunteers are those most likely to develop severe disease; only 2-3 more replication cycles would be needed to reach severe disease thresholds; and var switching rates are low in vitro though modeling suggests higher rates in vivo may be possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120, C123-C128 represent a thorough and critical discussion of study limitations and alternative interpretations. The authors appropriately critique prior work (C117), acknowledge their own limitations (C118), provide evidence that 3D7 retains switching capacity (C119-C120), and discuss the implications of the short study duration (C126). The discussion of switching rates (C127-C128) appropriately distinguishes between in vitro observations and in vivo possibilities. This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging limitations and uncertainties.
